{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nv-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"90955fb5641446577999fe8ee5e0cd1ee814da825e362ad72f897e118f7eb83a","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nv-class-c:lineage:19","source_registry_sha256":"3e184808e042e052d0c78d0dff47c50b34a56560f428649c492afe10bc7ba712","source_liveness_sha256":"0dfbf3aa4b4798b88d69252e076642b5f0a38751c5010711fbce93c8a7d6e292"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C2"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C2","chunk_id":"C2.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Right-of-way, speed and freeway confusables and continuation facts","heading":"C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: who yields first, yellow X versus red X, four-wheel versus rear-wheel ABS, braking time versus braking distance, and continuation facts on freeway lanes, ramp meters, exits and stopping distance","learner_facing":false,"markdown":"## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: who yields first, yellow X versus red X, four-wheel versus rear-wheel ABS, braking time versus braking distance, and continuation facts on freeway lanes, ramp meters, exits and stopping distance
Confusable pairs among the right-of-way, speed and freeway rules, followed by continuation facts that did not fit part C; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec05-R01 | anchor: A01
At an uncontrolled intersection the vehicle on the right usually goes first, but at a four-way stop the order is set by who arrived and stopped first. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; confusable uncontrolled intersection versus four-way stop.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R02 | anchor: A01
A left-turning driver yields to straight-through traffic already in the intersection, and a driver leaving a driveway or private road yields to everything on the main road, pedestrians included. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; confusable two yielding drivers.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-R03 | anchor: A02
Covering 15 miles at 70 mph rather than 60 mph saves just 2 minutes and 9 seconds, and a ticket costs both time and money. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R04 | anchor: A02
The posted limit is the upper bound for normal conditions, while the Basic Rule can demand a much lower speed when traffic, weather, visibility or the road surface call for it. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed; confusable posted limit versus Basic Rule.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-R05 | anchor: A03
Merging drivers must yield to traffic already on the freeway, while drivers already on it should watch for merging cars and adjust speed so merges stay smooth. [A03]
Why it matters: group freeway; confusable merging versus through driver.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-R06 | anchor: A03
Before any freeway lane change, check the mirrors and glance over your shoulder at the blind spot, use your turn signal, and watch for other drivers' signals. [A03]
Why it matters: group freeway; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-R07 | anchor: A04
On an on-ramp with more than one lane, each lane has its own meter, and drivers are encouraged to use both lanes and follow the meter for their own lane. [A04]
Why it matters: group ramp meters; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-R08 | anchor: A04
A yellow X still lets you use the lane, with care for slow traffic or debris or to prepare to merge out, whereas a red X closes the lane entirely. [A04]
Why it matters: group lane-use signals; confusable yellow X versus red X.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-R09 | anchor: A04
Overhead freeway signals show reduced speed limits and lane closures for construction, debris or crashes, update as you get closer, and show the lanes open again after the incident. [A04]
Why it matters: group lane-use signals; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-R10 | anchor: A05
HOV lanes exist to reward ridesharing and public transit, take congestion out of the regular lanes and improve overall traffic flow. [A05]
Why it matters: group HOV; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec05-R11 | anchor: A06
Most freeway exits are numbered, and the same numbers usually appear on the major freeway signs, which helps you spot your exit early. [A06]
Why it matters: group exits; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-R12 | anchor: A06
You can tell whether a car has ABS from a lit ABS symbol on the dashboard just after starting the engine, from the owner's manual, or by asking the dealer. [A06]
Why it matters: group ABS; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-R13 | anchor: A06
During ABS braking, do not jerk or crank the steering wheel hard, since that can send the vehicle onto the shoulder or emergency lane; steer back into your lane once the hazard is clear. [A06]
Why it matters: group ABS; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-R14 | anchor: A06
Four-wheel ABS keeps every wheel from locking, while rear-wheel ABS, found only on some light trucks, protects just the rear wheels; if the front wheels lock, ease off the pedal until they roll again. [A06]
Why it matters: group ABS; confusable four-wheel versus rear-wheel ABS.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec05-R15 | anchor: A07
Stopping distance depends on vehicle type and weight, speed, tire and brake condition, road surface, reaction time, alertness or fatigue, and the weather. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-R16 | anchor: A07
Perception is seeing and understanding why you must stop, reaction is the brain telling the foot to brake; together with moving the foot they make up perception and reaction distance. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping; confusable perception versus reaction.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-R17 | anchor: A07
Braking time is how long the brakes and tire-road friction need to stop the vehicle, while braking distance is how far it travels during that time. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping; confusable braking time versus braking distance.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-R18 | anchor: A07
On a wet road stopping distance can be more than double the dry figure, and the first rain of a season is especially dangerous because oil mixes with water on the pavement. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-R19 | anchor: A07
At 30 mph on ice the stopping distance would be 373 feet, more than the length of a football field. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-R20 | anchor: A07
For a typical car on dry, level pavement with a 2.5 second reaction time, stopping from 25 mph takes about 127 feet in all: 92 feet of perception and reaction plus 35 feet of braking. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping table; difficulty high.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec05-R21 | anchor: A07
In the same table, stopping from 45 mph takes about 278 feet in all, made up of 165 feet of perception and reaction distance and 113 feet of braking distance. [A07]
Why it matters: group stopping table; difficulty high.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0041]
